title: Cat Power - Breaking and Entering
summary: Cat power joins Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler on Breaking and Entering
transcript:
In May 2018, Chan Marshall joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler at Triple R ahead of Cat Power's Moon Pix twentieth-anniversary performance at Vivid LIVE. She reflects on recording the album with Jim White and Mick Turner, returning to its songs and the experiences behind them. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Chan Marshall, who is Cat Power, is in the country for a one-off show exclusive to Vivid LIVE at the Sydney Opera House, celebrating the twentieth anniversary of Moon Pix. She'll be playing the album in full with original collaborators Jim White and Mick Turner from Dirty Three, and Ned Collette is arranging the string segment. Chan dropped by the Triple R studio first thing Monday morning. Moon Pix brought her to Australia for the first time twenty years ago, to Sing Sing Studios in Richmond. We began by asking what initially brought her here.

Chan: My boyfriend, I was partnered with Bill Callahan at that time of my life, and we were living down in South Carolina. He was coming over here to tour, and I had a record advance, I think it was $3,400, so I got my flight. I had already faxed Jim and Mick and asked, actually, I don't think Jim White had a fax machine, but Mick did. I faxed him and asked if he could ask Jim if they would be interested in recording on the record. I came to Australia, hung out with Bill for about, I don't know, a week, and then he had to go back to the States. I stayed for another two months and just travelled around. It was after New Year's, and it was like a week or some crazy, like five days before I was supposed to leave when I made the booking at Sing Sing. I went and saw different studios. I was with this guy, Matt. I don't remember his last name. I had like four days, and Mick and Jim came in. I had been used to improvisation at that point in my life. I guess that's how I learned to even feel free enough to perform, that improvisational sort of attitude. I think I toured for that record after it came out for maybe a year and a half, and then went in to record The Covers Record and just kind of never played those songs again after 1999, I guess.

Simon: That musical relationship between you, Jim White and Mick Turner is reflected on the record. People were fascinated by the interplay and unconventional arrangements. Can you tell us more about that dynamic?

Chan: Going backwards, I also haven't listened to the work, the songs, in a really long time, so I had to revisit it for this show coming up. Jim and Mick, Dirty Three, they're three separate universes musically. They compel one another. I felt safe and confident in their understanding the open quality that I wanted for the simplistic song structures that I had. I knew that they musically are able to move. They listen. Obviously, you can hear it on the recordings. They're listening, but they're also in their very own element creatively, which is a really perfect marriage there, sonically.

Lauren: We spoke before about Matt, the sound engineer at Sing Sing Richmond. There was a great story of his experience recording with you.

Chan: Can I have more reverb, please? Can I have more reverb? Excuse me, I'm sorry. Can I please have more reverb?

Lauren: He talks about the sympathetic understanding you had in the studio, your playing and the response of Jim and Mick, and vice versa, this harmony he observed in action. You've spoken about the distance you've had from the record. How does it feel to be returning not only to these songs but to this band?

Chan: My chest just went kind of—because it feels like a lifetime. A lifetime of memories. It feels almost like a birthday or some sort of holiday or Christmas special, you know how private those things are. I think we all have, in the period of that time personally, all the travelling and sort of life experiences we've all had and gone through and survived, having lost friends and different life changes and things. It never feels like time has passed, seeing them again, hanging out with them again. I was able to play with Jim for a while for the Jukebox tour. I'm not a happy performer or singer, whatever you call it, but the years that I spent with Jukebox, with Jim, I was happy for the first time singing. Returning back to these songs, playing with two people that I love, because I'm like ten years younger, so at the time when I met him I was always like ten years younger. But now I'm pushing fifty or whatever. It's very special because not everybody gets the opportunity to, I'm getting all emotional, not everybody gets the opportunity to go back to a place where they feel they started something and revisit it and share it again. I never anticipated or suspected that ever it would mean anything to anybody. Over these years, having done other records, there's been many, many times people have said, 'That record Moon Pix means so much to me.' So it's really an honour to be invited to do something that most people don't have the opportunity to revisit.

Lauren: The story of Moon Pix and its creation is pretty legendary: the experience of writing almost all the songs in one deeply unsettled night in rural South Carolina. We jump into the interview by asking Chan whether the memory of that night remains as vivid as ever for her.

Chan: Yeah. I think having experiences like that through those transformative early adult years, having had several of those experiences that are unexplainable, logically unexplainable. Maybe scientifically explainable by doctors, psychiatrist-type explainable. But the impact, I think, spiritually: I was so deeply impacted when I took a trip to Africa in '96, bearing witness to certain things that were very impactful, that when I returned back to America, I was really shaken by this sort of, I guess we have this pineal gland thing. I don't know if you know what I'm talking about, but there was just this other presence that I felt like I had opened up to or something. So yeah, that night was pretty unforgettable.

Simon: For those who don't know the story of how Moon Pix was created in that one night, would you mind describing it as you recall it?

Chan: Sure. I had spent a couple of weeks on my own in this farmhouse surrounded by fields. I just got woken up by this really loud classical music playing. I woke up like, it's so loud, but it was like a lucid dream. There was a voice that was inside. You could hear the actual album, vinyl playing. I know this sounds crazy. I looked, just my eyes looked, and the windows were black because it was the middle of the night, maybe 3 a.m., 3.30. There was just this guy's voice: 'Come and meet me in the field.' I was like, 'This is a dream. I'm going to wake up from it.' So I kind of lost consciousness to go back under, and I mumbled no in my head. He said, 'Now. Come meet me in the field now.' Anyway, it's a really long story. In building the courage to say no very confidently, that's what woke me up and sat me up. Then it felt like when you're a kid and your sister punches you in the stomach or something, and you feel that air gets sucked out of your stomach. It felt like the air got sucked out of my stomach. I just felt this almost like an earthquake feeling. Then I guess my mind's eye saw these sort of waves covering the earth. It was like thousand-foot waves from all around that were all black, solid waves. I ran around the house. When I turned on the lights, I could see them more defined, pressed up against the window. They were just like entities or whatever. I had every light on, and I went to the bedroom and got a tape recorder. I was afraid I would lose my mind or I would disappear, so I just made up these songs on cassette as a sort of evidence that maybe there's a sound of, I don't know, whatever would happen next. But that's that. Then the sun rose, and I got in my truck and drove to New York City. I stayed there for about a week, then came back, packed up the house, and that's when I went to Australia.

Simon: You've touched on the relationship people have with this album. It's not uncommon to read essays about how people have been positively affected by it. Its legacy is immense. Ahead of performing it in its entirety for Vivid, what's your own relationship with the record then and now, after that distance and time away?

Chan: Well, I hadn't thought about the origination of the songwriting until last night, when I was sent a clip of a journalist. Even just saying it again feels slightly painful to admit that. But in recording them, there was light that I was trying to give everything there. Visiting to play them again, there's nothing but strength and liberation, emotional, spiritual, psychological, whatever, liberation. I think that the past twenty years, whatever's happened around the world, just having a good spirit frame of mind and sincerity to feel like I can breathe more triumph into the words and the vibration.

Simon: So, capturing the essence of what they were to begin with, this positive triumph and resilience, but also imbuing them with the spirit, experience and wisdom you've gained over time?

Chan: I don't know if it's wisdom. Just great, great, great gratitude.

Simon: Re-inhabiting the songs, but also bringing yourself as you are now?

Chan: Yeah, of course.

Lauren: We jump into the last part of this interview, chatting about 'Metal Heart', a song that resonates strongly with Cat Power today.

Chan: I've been playing 'Metal Heart'. I re-recorded it for Jukebox, so I've been kind of keeping it in my pocket, my repertoire, for all this time. I've been changing the words a little bit near the end. When I was young, I hid a lot from the audience, whether it was my bangs, alcohol, whatever it was. I hid a lot from the eyes and the contact of the humans. I felt like just doing my word-song duty, facilitating the songs, was enough until I got sober and did The Greatest. Then I didn't have an instrument to play with, so I had nothing binding my hands. It's the first time I ever saw people, when I was touring for The Greatest. Now, when I sing 'Metal Heart', I try to make eye contact with as many people as I can and tell them that society doesn't really care about you. But you have to know that you're a human being, and you just have to know that you're a powerful entity alone or with friends or whatever. You are everything because you are your own everything.

Lauren: Finally, you're also working with Ned Collette, who was a guest on our show this week.

Chan: He has a new album.

Lauren: He does, yes. You're working with Ned on the string section for the Vivid LIVE show. Can you tell us about working with him and his element of the performance?

Chan: Well, I met him years ago, but I don't remember. I'm sure that I kind of remember, but we're meeting today. We had a few phone conversations, and we felt he was able to accomplish his ideas and what I felt I needed help with, with every song. I've heard a few things, and it sounds beautiful. I asked Mick, and Mick recommended Ned. I'm really excited to give it new—not new life, but almost to validate the album, because I never really looked back. Like I was saying before, I've always just survived from touring. The albums were just gracious opportunities. But I've always survived. My work is singing to people live. I guess to me, it feels great to give life back to something, so I don't know. Lucky me, surviving all these years or something. I'm sorry.

Lauren: We do have to say we're very sad we don't get to see these shows in Melbourne. Damn Vivid and their exclusive Sydney shows.

Simon: As Lauren mentioned before, we cannot express enough how grateful we are to you for coming in today.

Chan: Thank you. I'm grateful to you for believing in me or having me here and appreciating what I've done or whatever.
